pharm: Long-acting benzodiazepine that enhances the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA at the GABA-A receptor, producing anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant, and muscle-relaxant effects; animal studies show a 'taming' action on the limbic system without sedation at low doses.

summary: Chlordiazepoxide is a long-acting benzodiazepine used for anxiety, preoperative apprehension, and the management of acute alcohol withdrawal. It carries a class BOXED WARNING: concomitant use with opioids can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death; benzodiazepines also carry risks of abuse, misuse, addiction, physical dependence, and potentially life-threatening withdrawal (including seizures). It is habit-forming (DEA Schedule IV). Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants, and taper gradually to discontinue. Caution is needed in the elderly, in hepatic/renal impairment, and where impending depression or suicidal tendencies may be present.
indications: Management of anxiety disorders or short-term relief of symptoms of anxiety

Note: openFDA carries only the chlordiazepoxide + clidinium combination product (indicated to control emotional/somatic factors in GI disorders such as peptic ulcer and irritable bowel syndrome); monotherapy indications above are from the benzodiazepine label and standard references

moa: Chlordiazepoxide is a benzodiazepine that binds the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor complex, enhancing the affinity of GABA for the receptor and increasing chloride conductance. This potentiates GABA-mediated neuronal inhibition, producing anxiolytic, sedative-hypnotic, anticonvulsant, and skeletal-muscle-relaxant effects. Animal data indicate action on the limbic system with a 'taming' (reduction of fear/aggression) effect at doses below those causing sedation.

preg: Avoid. An increased risk of congenital malformations associated with minor tranquilizers (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, meprobamate) during the first trimester has been suggested in several studies. Because use is rarely urgent, it should almost always be avoided in pregnancy; advise women to inform their physician if they become or plan to become pregnant.
lact: Avoid. Benzodiazepines are excreted in breast milk and may cause sedation, poor feeding, or respiratory difficulty in the nursing infant. Weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against maternal need and consider monitoring the infant.
renal: Use the usual precautions in patients with impaired renal function; use the lowest effective dose with careful monitoring.
hepatic: Use caution in patients with impaired hepatic function; clearance is reduced and effects may be prolonged. Blood dyscrasias, jaundice, and hepatic dysfunction have occasionally been reported; periodic liver function tests are advisable with protracted therapy.

major: Opioids (boxed warning - profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death; limit dose and duration)
Other CNS depressants and alcohol (additive sedation/respiratory depression)
moderate: MAO inhibitors and phenothiazines (potentiation; concomitant psychotropic use generally not recommended)
Oral anticoagulants (variable effects on coagulation reported rarely with chlordiazepoxide)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid. Alcohol produces additive CNS and respiratory depression and increases the risk of serious adverse outcomes, overdose, and death.
interactions.diagnostics: Changes in EEG patterns (low-voltage fast activity) have been observed during and after therapy.

emergency: Severe respiratory depression / coma (especially with opioids or alcohol)

Signs of abuse, misuse, addiction, and developing tolerance

counsel: This medicine is habit-forming - take exactly as prescribed, do not increase the dose or take it longer than directed, and keep it secured away from others
Do not drink alcohol or use opioids/other sedating drugs without your provider's guidance - the combination can cause severe drowsiness, breathing problems, or death
Do not stop suddenly; the dose must be tapered to avoid serious withdrawal symptoms including seizures
It can cause drowsiness, dizziness, and impaired coordination - avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you
Avoid use in pregnancy and while breastfeeding; tell your provider if you are or may become pregnant
Report excessive sleepiness, slowed/shallow breathing, severe confusion, or unusual mood/behavior changes immediately
pk: Oral onset within ~1-2 hours; rapid CNS effect
Plasma peak generally within a few hours of an oral dose
Long-acting; parent and active metabolites have prolonged half-lives (often >24 h)
Long duration; accumulation with repeated dosing, especially in elderly/hepatic impairment
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light (unstable in solution)

openFDA only carries the chlordiazepoxide + clidinium combination product, so monotherapy dosing here is drawn from the benzodiazepine label and standard references; the boxed warning shown is the benzodiazepine class warning as it applies to chlordiazepoxide
Boxed warning: concomitant opioid use can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death
Taper gradually - abrupt discontinuation or flumazenil can precipitate life-threatening withdrawal (seizures); protracted withdrawal can last weeks to >12 months
Long half-life favors smoother withdrawal management (e.g., alcohol withdrawal) but causes accumulation in the elderly and hepatic impairment - start low
missed: If used on a fixed schedule and a dose is missed, take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it; do not double up. Do not abruptly stop the medication on your own - dependence can develop, so any discontinuation should be planned with your prescriber.
overdose: Manifestations of chlordiazepoxide overdose include somnolence, confusion, diminished reflexes, and coma. Monitor respiration, pulse, and blood pressure. Provide general supportive measures, maintain an adequate airway, and give IV fluids; gastric lavage may be used. Hypotension may be treated with vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine). Flumazenil, a benzodiazepine antagonist, may reverse effects but can precipitate seizures/withdrawal in dependent patients and is used with caution. Dialysis is of limited value; consider co-ingestants, especially other CNS depressants.
